extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical writers, and students (authors, lecturers, readers of mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical criteria for reading, writing, and lecturing mathematics (how to present, revise, and guide readers/listeners). Drawn from Halmos's autobiography-derived advice about mathematical practice and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active-reading six-question test
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't just read it; fight it! Ask your own questions, look for your own examples, discover your own proofs. The six questions: (1) Is the hypothesis necessary? (2) Is the converse true? (3) What happens in the classical special case? (4) What about the degenerate cases? (5) Where does the proof use the hypothesis? (6) Construct your own examples and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reader cannot answer these questions, they have not understood the text. By symmetry, a piece of mathematics that prevents the reader from answering these questions is poorly written. Use these questions as a checklist when reading or when judging whether exposition is clear and illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say Something (Substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To have something to say is by far the most important ingredient of good exposition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance is primary: technical polish, notation, or formal completeness cannot substitute for actually having a non-trivial point. Evaluate whether the work conveys a meaningful new idea or insight rather than merely producing correct but empty results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral-writing / revise repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality emerges from re-writing: write a section, set it aside, return to it, rewrite it again, often many times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good piece of mathematical writing should show signs of revision — coherent organization, stable terminology across sections, and the absence of visible first-draft false starts. Prefer iterative rewriting over trying to perfect a first draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum-resistance organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material "to minimize the resistance and maximize the insight of the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For every presentational choice, ask whether the ordering, notation, or proof structure makes the reader's path easier or harder. Choose orderings, notations, and proof structures that reveal the idea rather than hide it; avoid arrangements that force the reader through unnecessary cognitive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship model: guide the reader like a master
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is learned by doing alongside a master; good exposition acts as a master would, guiding the reader through the moves, motivation, and pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposition should not merely present results: include motivation, explain choices made, point out common pitfalls, and guide readers through the sequence of ideas as a mentor would in an apprenticeship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture as preparation, not proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A lecture is not a proof — it is preparation for the listener to study the proof later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lecture should convey the main idea and convince that the proof works without delivering every detail. It should prepare listeners to fill in details on their own; do not attempt to transcribe full proofs into a talk that is meant to motivate and orient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show evidence of revision in the visible text
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematical writing should show signs of revision — coherent organization, no false starts in the visible text, terminology stable across sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a manuscript, look for polished flow and consistent terminology; visible drafts, meandering exposition, or unresolved false starts indicate insufficient revision and lower quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretentious rigor (empty formalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretentious rigor without substance — formal or pedantic presentation that lacks an interesting point — is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake elaborate formalism for depth. Prefer clarity and meaningful content over showing off technical completeness when that completeness doesn't illuminate the main idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid order-of-discovery organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Order-of-discovery organization — presenting a proof in the sequence it was found rather than the order that helps the reader — is an anti-pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorganize material to present the clearest logical development for the reader, even if that hides the path the author originally took. Present proofs in the order that maximizes insight, not the author's historical chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid notation overload
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive or unnecessary notation that adds nothing is counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use notation only when its payoff (clarity, concision) justifies the cognitive cost. Introduce notation sparingly and prefer simple expressions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide motivation for definitions (avoid reverence for definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverence for definitions without motivation is criticized; definitions should not be presented as sacred objects divorced from why they matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing definitions, explain their purpose, provide intuition and examples, and show how they arise naturally from the problems being addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't mistake length for depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaking length for depth — equating long or elaborate exposition with substantive understanding — is an anti-pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the conceptual content rather than page count. Clear, concise exposition that conveys deep ideas is preferable to long-windedness that obscures rather than illuminates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, direct, conversational prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Halmos preferred simple, direct, conversational prose: the best mathematical writing reads like a thoughtful person explaining something they care about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write as if explaining to an intelligent colleague: use plain language, avoid unnecessary formality, and aim for a tone that communicates interest and clarity rather than bureaucratic distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied composite rubric for good mathematical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematical exposition is good to the extent that it: has something to say (substance); survives the six-question test; shows evidence of revision; minimizes reader resistance; acts like a master apprenticing the reader; and distinguishes lecture from proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this composite list as an overall evaluative checklist: each item addresses a different dimension (content, clarity, organization, pedagogy, and register). A strong exposition scores well across these dimensions rather than only on formal correctness.
